query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Controlled hydrogen charging of a eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 high-entropy alloy will reduce the stacking fault energy, promote enhanced deformation-induced nanotwinning at the lamellar internal boundaries, and therefore simultaneously improve yield strength and room-temperature tensile ductility relative to the conventional as-cast lamellar microstructure.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 high-entropy alloy featuring dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal (phase) boundaries prone to microcracking.
generation.intervention: Application of controlled hydrogen charging via electrochemical methods to achieve an optimized diffusible hydrogen concentration (~50–100 ppm).
generation.conditions: Room-temperature hydrogen charging in a controlled atmosphere (e.g., electrochemical charging with specified current density and duration) to precisely obtain the target hydrogen concentration without causing embrittlement.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced nanotwin formation along the lamellar interfaces.
generation.mechanism: Hydrogen lowers the stacking fault energy in the matrix, thereby promoting the nucleation and proliferation of deformation-induced nanotwins. These nanotwins act as effective barriers to crack nucleation and propagation, and also promote greater work hardening, leading to simultaneous increases in yield strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified lamellar baseline, the hydrogen-charged alloy is expected to demonstrate a higher yield strength (due to increased work hardening from nanotwin formation) as well as improved room-temperature tensile ductility owing to effective crack arrest at the internal boundaries.
generation.baseline: Conventional as-cast eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies that exhibit intrinsic brittleness and limited room-temperature ductility due to microcrack initiation at internal boundaries.
generation.boundary: The benefits are expected to occur within a limited hydrogen concentration window (~50–100 ppm). Exceeding this optimal range may lead to hydrogen embrittlement, while insufficient hydrogen may not achieve the desired level of nanotwinning.
generation.uncertainty: There remains uncertainty regarding the precise optimal hydrogen concentration and distribution uniformity, as well as the long-term stability of the induced nanotwin microstructure under cyclic or prolonged loading conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of as-cast eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloys. Subject one batch to controlled hydrogen charging under the specified conditions (electrochemical charging to achieve ~50–100 ppm hydrogen concentration) while using the other batch as an unmodified control. Perform standardized room-temperature tensile tests on both batches alongside microstructural characterization (using TEM/ECCI) to assess nanotwin density at the internal lamellar boundaries.
measurements: Diffusible hydrogen concentration (ppm) using hydrogen desorption analysis
Room-temperature yield strength and uniform elongation via tensile testing
Nanotwin density and microstructural features at lamellar boundaries using high-resolution TEM/ECCI
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the hydrogen-charged samples do not exhibit statistically significant increases in both yield strength and tensile ductility relative to the control, or if no corresponding increase in nanotwin density is observed, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:Strength and ductility upon hydrogen charging
cited_evidence.text: On the contrary, the alloy pre-charged for 12 h and in-situ tensile tested with a current density of 15 mA·cm−2 (curve #2) shows a notable increase of both, ultimate tensile strength (571 MPa) and uniform elongation (~71%) compared to the sample tested without any preceding hydrogen alloying. Note that the diffusible hydrogen concentration in the sample under this condition (12 h pre-charged at a current density of 15 mA·cm−2) was determined to be 8.01 wt.ppm according to the hydrogen desorption rate curves (Supplementary Fig. 2). Moreover, as the diffusible hydrogen concentration increased to 15.22 wt.ppm (72 h pre-charged at a current density of 25 mA·cm−2) (curve #3), the ultimate tensile strength and uniform elongation are 588 MPa and ~71%, respectively, which are ~7.9% and ~4.4% larger, respectively, than those observed for the same alloy without hydrogen (curve #1). With further increasing the diffusible hydrogen concentration to 33.25 wt.ppm (240 h pre-charged at a current density of 100 mA·cm−2), the HEA (curve #4) shows a slightly reduced increment in its ultimate strength and uniform elongation compared to the alloy with a hydrogen concentration of 15.22 wt.ppm (curve #3)

To reveal the micro-mechanisms behind the hydrogen induced joint increase in both, strength and ductility, we probed the deformation microstructures in the cross-sections of the CoCrFeMnNi HEA samples tensile tested under various hydrogen charging conditions. Figure 4 shows the typical ECC images of the microstructure near the fracture surfaces of the HEAs samples both with and without hydrogen charging. A few deformation nanotwins in the CoCrFeMnNi HEA sample without hydrogen were observed (Fig. 4a), which is consistent with a previous study which showed that deformation twining can occur in this HEA at relatively high strain levels at room temperature. Interestingly, we observe that the density of nanotwins in the hydrogen alloyed HEA sample significantly increased compared to the hydrogen free alloy (Fig. 4 and Supplementary Fig. 5). For instance, as shown in Fig. 4b, the sample with a diffusible hydrogen concentration of 15.22 wt.ppm (72 h pre-charged at a current density of 25 mA·cm−2) shows a very high density of nanotwins compared to the HEA without hydrogen. We reveal the nanotwinning here by ECCI analysis using bulk samples to avoid any thin slice size and related effects

The equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA has a relatively low intrinsic stacking fault energy (~19 mJ·m2), which explains the occurrence of mechanical twinning at room temperature without hydrogen charging. The strong increase in twinning density in the hydrogen alloyed HEA samples reveals that hydrogen reduces the stacking fault energy of the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA. This is consistent with the previous studies on the effect of hydrogen on the stacking fault energy in other f.c.c. structured alloys, . Moreover, no other phase formed during the in-situ tensile testing with hydrogen charging according to the XRD results shown in Supplementary Fig. 6. These results also show that the increase in the density of nanotwins that we observe in the CoCrFeMnNi HEA leads to an associated increase in work hardening (Supplementary Fig. 3), which postpones the formation of geometric instabilities to higher strain values, thereby increasing strength and ductility simultaneously.

proposals.intervention: Controlled hydrogen charging (at a specific, optimized concentration)
proposals.conditions: Room-temperature hydrogen charging in a controlled atmosphere (e.g. electrochemical charging under ambient conditions with a controlled current density and time to achieve a target hydrogen concentration of ~50–100 ppm)
proposals.structural_mediator: Enhanced nanotwin formation along the lamellar internal boundaries
proposals.mechanism: Hydrogen lowers the stacking fault energy in the matrix, which promotes nanotwinning during deformation. These twins arrest microcrack nucleation and propagation at the internal lamellar interfaces while also increasing work hardening, thus enhancing both tensile strength and ductility.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified lamellar baseline, the hydrogen-charged alloy is expected to exhibit a higher yield strength (due to increased work hardening) together with improved room-temperature tensile ductility as nanotwins act as crack arresters.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This single intervention targets the microcrack initiation sites at internal boundaries by modifying the deformation mechanism (via nanotwinning) and thereby overcomes the typical strength–ductility trade-off in eutectic high-entropy alloys.

proposals.intervention: Optimized thermomechanical processing via cryo-rolling followed by controlled low-temperature annealing
proposals.conditions: Apply a two-stage deformation: first cryo-rolling at ~−196 °C to introduce fine-scale defects and stored energy, followed by rapid annealing at ~600–700 °C for a short duration (e.g. 30–60 s) to facilitate partial recovery and interface bonding without coarsening the lamellae.
proposals.structural_mediator: Refined ultrafine duplex microstructure that retains the inherent lamellar colony but with strengthened and more coherent internal boundaries
proposals.mechanism: The severe deformation at cryogenic temperatures creates a high density of defects that, when partially annealed, evolve into a dual-phase microstructure. The optimized process both imparts grain refinement and enhances the bond strength at internal boundaries, inhibiting early microcrack formation.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Relative to the conventional cast lamellar baseline, the processed alloy is predicted to show a significant increase in yield strength (due to grain refinement and defect strengthening) while achieving higher tensile ductility via improved damage tolerance from strengthened boundaries.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By carefully tailoring the thermomechanical history, this intervention overcomes the brittleness inherent in coarse lamellar colonies by simultaneously enhancing interfacial cohesion and refining the microstructure.

proposals.material_system: Eutectic high-entropy alloy based on AlCoCrFeNi system
proposals.intervention: Minor alloying addition of a large atomic radius element (e.g. Zr)
proposals.conditions: Introduce Zr in small amounts (e.g. 3–7 at.%) during casting and subsequent homogenization heat treatment at ~900 °C to ensure uniform solid solution and favorable segregation at the lamellar interfaces
proposals.structural_mediator: Enhanced lattice distortion and improved interfacial coherency within lamellar colonies
proposals.mechanism: The addition of Zr increases lattice distortion and induces solid solution strengthening while also segregating to the internal boundaries, which improves the coherence and bonding between lamellae. This suppresses microcrack initiation along the boundaries during tensile loading.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to the Zr-free eutectic alloy, the Zr-modified alloy is expected to display higher yield strength owing to improved solid solution and interfacial strengthening, as well as increased tensile ductility through reduction in premature microcrack propagation.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This single compositional modification shifts the strength–ductility balance favorably by improving interlamellar bonding and increasing resistance to interfacial cracking, directly addressing the brittleness issue.

proposals.intervention: Tailored rapid annealing to induce in situ formation of ultra-thin, coherent B2 nanoprecipitates along lamellar boundaries
proposals.conditions: Subject the as-cast lamellar alloy to a rapid heating–cooling cycle: heat rapidly (e.g. at 15 K/s) to an optimal annealing temperature (~850 °C) and hold for a very short time (30–50 s) before rapid quenching, ensuring localized precipitation along boundaries
proposals.structural_mediator: In situ formed, ultrathin, coherent B2 nanoprecipitates selectively decorating the lamellar interfaces
proposals.mechanism: The rapid annealing creates a supersaturated state that triggers controlled precipitation at the energetically favorable sites—the lamellar boundaries. These coherent precipitates hinder microcrack nucleation and blunt crack propagation, while also contributing to overall strengthening through particle dispersion strengthening.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified baseline, the annealed alloy is predicted to maintain or exceed the original yield strength while exhibiting significantly improved tensile ductility due to the crack-arresting influence of the nanoprecipitates.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This intervention directly targets the weak internal boundaries by introducing a nano-scale reinforcement that improves both strength and ductility, providing a single, unified solution to the microcracking problem.

decision.rationale: Direction A, which employs controlled hydrogen charging to promote nanotwinning, directly addresses the dual challenge of increasing strength (via enhanced work hardening) and improving tensile ductility (by arresting crack propagation) in eutectic high-entropy alloys. The supporting evidence from prior studies (e.g., PMC5575320 records) clearly illustrates that moderate hydrogen charging can reduce stacking fault energy, thereby inducing a denser nanotwin network that benefits both strength and ductility. Compared to processing routes that involve additional deformation steps (B), compositional modifications (C), or complex precipitate engineering (D), the hydrogen charging intervention is a single, controllable modification that targets the critical internal boundaries responsible for microcrack initiation. Thus, we choose to adopt direction A.
